# Packets, Frames, Encapsulation

Data is **wrapped** in headers as it descends the stack and **unwrapped** on the way up. Clear names prevent confusion in captures and design talks.

## Learning goals

- Use correct terms: data, segment/datagram, packet, frame  
- Sketch encapsulation for a simple TCP and UDP flow  
- Read a tcpdump line and identify outer headers  
- Explain how tunnels add outer encapsulations  

## Vocabulary

| Term | Layer (typical) | Meaning |
|------|-----------------|---------|
| **Data / payload** | Application | What the app cares about |
| **Segment** | TCP | TCP header + payload |
| **Datagram** | UDP (and sometimes IP) | UDP header + payload |
| **Packet** | IP | IP header + payload |
| **Frame** | Link | Ethernet (or other) header + payload + FCS |

People say “packet” loosely; in precise talk, **frame** is L2 and **packet** is L3.

## Encapsulation path (send)

1. Application writes bytes  
2. Transport adds **src/dst ports** (TCP adds seq/ack/flags)  
3. IP adds **src/dst IP**, TTL, protocol  
4. Ethernet adds **src/dst MAC**, Ethertype  
5. Bits go on the wire (or veth)  

```
 Application data
+------------------+
| TCP/UDP header   |
+------------------+
| IP header        |
+------------------+
| Ethernet header  |
+------------------+
```

## Decapsulation path (receive)

Reverse order: FCS check → MAC → Ethertype → IP → protocol → ports → app.

## Maximum sizes and MTU

- **MTU**: max IP packet size a link will accept (commonly 1500 on Ethernet)  
- Oversized IPv4 packets may be fragmented if allowed, or dropped with fragmentation-needed feedback; IPv6 routers return Packet Too Big rather than fragmenting.  
- Tunnel encapsulation consumes underlay capacity; a VLAN tag increases frame size and does not necessarily reduce IP MTU when the link supports tagged frames.  

Details and labs: Layer 3 ICMP/PMTU chapter later; foundations need the idea.

## Captures: reading the onion

```bash
# On a Linux lab node
tcpdump -ni eth1 -vv
tcpdump -ni eth1 icmp
tcpdump -ni eth1 'tcp port 22'
```

What you see first is the **outer** header. Inner headers appear after decap or when capturing on the right interface.

## Tunnels and overlays (preview)

Overlays wrap an **inner** packet in an **outer** IP/UDP (or GRE) packet. Underlay routers only need to forward the outer packet. Full treatment: Overlays part.

```
[ Outer Eth | Outer IP | Outer UDP | VXLAN | Inner Eth | Inner IP | … ]
```

## Lab sketch (two nodes)

1. Deploy two Linux nodes on one L2 segment  
2. Capture while `ping` runs — ICMP inside IP inside Ethernet  
3. Capture `nc` or `curl` — TCP three-way handshake fields  

## Worked packet walk: local and remote destinations

Assume host A is `192.0.2.10/24`, its gateway is `192.0.2.1`, and host B is `198.51.100.20`. A chooses the gateway because B is outside the connected prefix. It resolves **192.0.2.1**, not B, with ARP. Its Ethernet frame has A's source MAC and the gateway's destination MAC, while the IP header still has A and B as source and destination. At the router the incoming frame is removed and a new outgoing frame is constructed. The IP source and destination normally stay unchanged, but TTL decreases; NAT or tunneling can change the observed headers.

If B were `192.0.2.20`, A would normally resolve B directly and send a frame to B's MAC. A frame's destination MAC is a next-hop address on one link; it is not a globally meaningful end-to-end address. Switches forward the existing frame within a broadcast domain, while routers create a new link-layer frame for the next link.

### Size arithmetic and capture caveats

With an IPv4 MTU of 1500 and no IPv4 or TCP options, at most 1460 bytes remain for TCP data in one IP packet: `1500 − 20 IPv4 − 20 TCP = 1460`. IPv6's base header is 40 bytes, so the equivalent is 1440 before extension headers or TCP options. Ethernet headers and FCS are outside that IP MTU. A VLAN tag increases Ethernet frame overhead; whether it reduces available IP MTU depends on the link's supported frame size. Tunnels add outer headers, so their inner MTU must fit the underlay.

IPv4 routers may fragment when allowed, but a packet with Don't Fragment set must instead be dropped if too large, normally with an ICMP fragmentation-needed message. IPv6 routers do not fragment packets; the source uses Packet Too Big feedback and may fragment at the source. Blocking that feedback can create a path-MTU black hole. See [RFC 8200](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8200.html) and [RFC 8900](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8900.html).

A host capture may show packets before segmentation or after receive aggregation because of offloads, and apparent checksum errors can occur before hardware completes a checksum. Ethernet FCS is often not supplied to the capture at all. Capture at both endpoints or on an intermediate link before assuming the capture is a literal wire image.


## Checkpoint

Draw encapsulation for **DNS over UDP** and **SSH over TCP** from host A to B on the same Ethernet. Label every header.
